subject: mimicChest
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: treasure-chest mimic with a long tongue.
Style: Dungeons & Dragons.
reasoning:
I'm designing a classic D&D-style treasure-chest mimic: a wooden chest with iron bands and a lock that reveals itself as a toothy maw with a long slimy tongue, pseudopods, and eyes.

For the rig, I'm treating the lid as the upper jaw and the chest base as the lower jaw/body, with a hinge joint for the jaw role, a tentacle-role chain for the tongue, and stubby pseudopod legs — maybe four stumpy clawed limbs plus a couple of side tentacle-arms to keep the silhouette cohesive.

The chest itself is wooden with iron bands and corner brackets, the domed lid hinged at the back and opened 50-60° to expose the maw lined with fleshy pink-red tissue, upper teeth along the lid's edge, lower teeth along the base's rim, and a dark throat behind. A long sinuous tongue (~1.6m) curls out in an S-curve onto the floor, slick with papillae bumps and a central groove, tip curling upward. I'm skipping distinct eyes since mimics typically don't have them.

Though it risks breaking the chest silhouette, I'll keep it simple and readable: two big eyes near the top front of the lid, above where the lock plate typically sits at the base/lid seam.

Actually, thinking through the geometry of an open lid tilting back on its hinge, the front face would foreshorten and tilt upward, making eyes placed there awkward to see from the front. I'm considering instead placing the eyes on the interior underside of the lid, like the roof of a mouth.

For composition: the open lid reveals its underside like the upper part of a mouth with teeth hanging along the front edge, the base acting as the lower jaw with its own teeth, and a tongue draping down the front and curling at the floor. I'll place two large glaring eyes on the lid's interior near the front hinge edge so they read clearly from a front-and-slightly-above viewing angle.

Four stubby legs under the chest completes the classic look. For the eyes, I'll recess them on the interior of the lid near the front edge, glaring out from under a brow-like ridge once open, and I need to nail down the lid's open-pose geometry to place them right. I'll set real-world dimensions too — a treasure chest roughly 1m wide, 0.6m deep, 0.6m tall with a domed lid — sized as Medium but scaled up a bit for a suitably long, impressive tongue.

I'm scaling up to about 1.2m wide, 0.75m deep, 0.5m base height plus 0.2m legs and a 0.3m dome, working out that with the lid open around 55-60°, total height comes to roughly 1.5m and the tongue should extend to 1.6-2m. Now I'm figuring out the rotation axis and sign convention for the hinge bone so opening the lid lifts the front edge upward correctly.

So the safer approach is building everything in closed pose first, then posing the lid at the end, since the tongue emerges from the base unaffected. There's also a skinning subtlety: parts built on the lid inherit its bone, and paint gets baked into position at build time, staying fixed through later poses.

Now I'm thinking through the chest itself - it needs to be a box with an open top, and the interior should read as a hollow shell with visible, thick walls when the lid swings open.

I want the mouth to read as a monster's maw: red fleshy floor with a darker throat area toward the back, maybe a dark disc or cylinder suggesting depth, and pink ridged gum slabs along the inside rim where the teeth emerge. I'll keep the geometry simple to manage complexity.

For the box's outer shell, I'm planning wall boxes with wood-painted exteriors and thin flesh-colored lining slabs inset just inside them, plus a bottom floor box -- doubling parts but keeping each face paintable separately, in keeping with the blocky low-poly primitive style expected for the puppet.

For the lid, I want the classic barrel-vault treasure chest shape: a half-cylinder extrusion along the chest's width using a semicircular profile in the YZ plane, so the flat ends form caps and the underside stays flat for sitting on the shell.

I'll keep this solid (efficient, since you only see the underside and end caps when open), but paint it differently by surface: wood outside, flesh-colored underside, using a normal-based check so the palate color only appears where the normal points downward in the closed pose.

I realize the half-pipe would leave open ends, so I'd need semicircle end caps acting as wooden planks with iron trim to close the cavity. Actually maybe a lathe shape spun around the X axis would be a simpler way to build the lid instead of this arch-extrude approach.

Lathe can't produce a half-cylinder though, so I need to stick with extruding the arch band plus separate end plates, then add iron reinforcement bands (slightly larger arcs extruded thin along X) at the ends and center, plus a front lip. For the teeth, I'm reasoning through orientation — in the closed pose the hinge sits at the back-top of the base, the lid's interior faces down, so the upper teeth should hang from the lid's front rim pointing downward.

Working out the rotation: when the lid opens by about 60°, that downward tooth direction rotates about the X-axis, and running the trig shows the teeth end up pointing forward-and-down rather than straight down, which I'm checking against where the lid's front edge physically moves relative to the hinge.

So the opened lid swings up with its front edge still ahead of the hinge, and the upper teeth now hang forward-down toward the viewer, matching how a monster's fangs look in an open-mouth pose, with the lower teeth standing up from the base's front edge to meet them.

For the ring of teeth, I want a mix: bigger fangs at front, smaller molar-like teeth along the sides, using simple cone geometry stuck into the gums for a cheap, irregular, jagged D&D-style look with varied sizes and slightly yellowed ivory coloring, roughly 14 upper and 14 lower for 28 total.

For legs, I'm picturing four short, stubby, beast-like paws (almost lion-paw feet) sprouting from the chest for a playful, mimic-appropriate feel rather than tentacle pseudopods.

I'll keep the core elements—legs, pseudopod arms, tongue, lid, eyes—and have the stubby legs raise the chest about 0.22m off the ground so it reads clearly as a creature rather than furniture.

For the legs, I'm picturing thick clawed paws in a fleshy purple-brown tone. For color palette, I'm thinking warm wood browns, iron grey-blue, brass trim, a blood-red mouth, purplish-grey flesh, ivory teeth, slit-pupiled yellow eyes, and gold coins with colored gems—possibly stuck to the mimic's body since mimics are known to have adhesive skin that traps items.

A few coins and gems stuck to the body, tongue, or heaped inside the mouth as bait feels like a defensible small detail tied to the mimic's identity rather than unrelated scenery. I'm now planning the tongue as a long articulated chain of about ten segments acting like a tentacle, emerging from the rear interior of the mouth and arcing up over the front rim.

It then droops down toward the floor in a lolling S-curve extending roughly 1.5 meters forward, tip curling slightly upward, resting on or just hovering above the ground to satisfy the floor-contact rule.

For the cross-section I'll give the tongue a flattened, elliptical shape that's wide and thin — broad near the base, narrowing toward a spade-like tip — giving it a convincing fleshy ribbon look rather than a cylindrical shape.

Actually, I like the idea of a gold coin stuck to the sticky tongue tip for comic effect, with a spatulate tip, a notch, tiny papillae bumps, and a darker midline groove painted along the sweep angle.

I'm figuring out how the dorsal clock orientation stays consistent as the tongue curves from flat-on-floor to vertical near the mouth, using world-up as the reference. I also want the underside paler than the glossy, darker saturated top, brightened near upward-facing surfaces to fake a wet sheen since specular isn't available. Now I'm moving on to eye placement, going for a beholder-lite look with two large main eyes plus smaller ones positioned near the top-front of the lid.

For the eyes I'm checking how the lid's underside orientation looks from the viewer's angle when the lid opens 60°, computing the rotated normal vector to confirm it faces forward-and-down enough that the palate surface (and any eyes placed there) stays visible from a front three-quarter or slightly elevated camera position.

I'm now planning the eye geometry itself: small spheres half-embedded in the lid's palate, oriented so their "front" points along the palate's surface normal, with iris and slit-pupil details applied as a texture decal on each sphere.

Checking the decal API signature...

I'd rather use the decal approach for precise eyeball placement than a full sphere texture. Stepping back, I want to make sure the face gets settled first—eyes readable from the front, a muzzle shaping the head, ears and brows scaled to the head constant—before anything else like hats or weapons gets placed in front of them.

Thinking through depth ordering: the tongue projects forward from the lower jaw, the upper teeth sit at the lid's front edge, and the eyes sit further back inside the lid above the teeth line, so nothing blocks them as long as placement is right. I want the eyes prominent, so I'll put them roughly mid-lid along its 0.8m depth, around x = ±0.22.

For brow ridges, I'm adding stout angular wedges in dark flesh above each eye, slanted inward-down for an angry look, with a half-sphere eyelid cap tilted to match. I'm also considering a design flourish where the lock's hasp sits on the lid's outer face and the keyhole on the base could double as a creepy little eye.

The idea is that from the back and sides, the chest should look like a totally ordinary treasure chest—wooden planks, iron bands, brass lock plate, corner brackets, ring handles, studs—while the front/inside reveals the monster. For the legs, I'm sketching fleshy purple-grey monster legs with ridged skin and claws replacing the classic corner feet, and I'm setting rough dimensions for the base box and leg placement.

Now I'm working out the lid geometry: hinged at the back, a domed barrel-arch shape about 0.7 long and roughly 0.26-0.3 high, trying to describe its curved profile as a flattened semicircle or superellipse so it can be extruded properly.

The lid should be slightly wider than the base to overhang it, and when opened to around 60°, the top of the whole chest ends up near 1.38 m, giving a model height of about 1.4 m, which feels right for good visibility into the interior.

For the legs, I'm placing them inset at the four base corners, splayed outward crab-style with feet positioned further out than the hips so they look stubby and bent given the short vertical space available. I'll use a two-segment IK limb setup so each leg bends naturally from hip to knee to foot on the ground.

For the paw, I'm adding a flattened lobe with three forward-pointing claw toes built from a chain structure.

I'll keep each toe simple: one joint per toe with a "digit" role, paired with a capsule sweep and a claw spike, built through a small helper function so I can reuse it for each foot.

Given the limits, I need to budget carefully — 1000 parts, 60k triangles, 160 joints, and only 64 flat colors (since paints don't count against that). I'll rely mostly on paints and keep a tight palette of around 25 flat colors. For the arms, I'm considering two pseudopod-style limbs with a shoulder, elbow, and wrist, ending in either a sucker pad with tiny finger-nubs or a simpler tentacle shape for charm.

I keep going back and forth — maybe skip arms entirely and just do legs, tongue, eyes, and the lid, since arms add complexity. But two side pseudopods really sell the "mimic" vibe, so I'll sprout them as curved tentacle chains from the base's side walls, extending outward with bulbous ends, tiny finger tentacles, and sucker discs along the underside in purple-grey flesh with cream-colored suckers. I'm working out how to sprout this chain from the wall surface using a path-based sweep with adjustable radius and segment count.

Now I'm scoping the overall build: targeting 180–340 parts, 5–12 textures, 700–1100 lines of code, written carefully since I have no way to test it directly. I need to be meticulous about API correctness — avoiding self-intersecting outlines in extrude calls, keeping lathe outlines non-negative on x, matching chain names to path spans, using sprout and decal/cards/svg textures properly, naming unused paint callback parameters with underscores, and ensuring all joint names stay unique.

I'm also confirming how `rng(seed)` works — it returns a random number generator function rather than a value, so it gets passed as `rand` or `rng` into scatter/tiling functions. I'm mapping out the full set of SDK exports (builder, frame, geometry helpers, texture utilities, color/noise functions) and the separate kit modules like glow and clockwork that get imported from their own paths.

Good, kit imports are confirmed to work per the docs, so I'll use the `glow` kit for self-lit surfaces, and possibly the `clockwork` kit's metal paint for iron bands, keeping risk low by sticking to small, well-documented additions.

Weighing the tradeoff: `metal` gives rich procedural tarnish/sheen effects I could otherwise hand-roll with noise in a few lines, but if the kit path doesn't resolve, the whole module breaks—high risk for modest gain. Still, the guidance suggests these kit helpers are the tested, reliable approach.

I also need `glow` for the gems and eyes to self-illuminate, which is really just setting emissive properties on the material—trivial enough that I consider inlining my own copy instead of importing the kit, since that avoids any risk of a broken import while producing identical results. But the documented import path seems reliable enough that I lean toward trusting the kit rather than duplicating its logic myself.

For the overall D&D aesthetic, I'm thinking rich painterly fantasy tones—wood, iron, gold, gems, a blood-red maw—built with custom paint shaders and warm top-lighting against cooler shadows, rather than a toon style. I'll likely combine the kit's `glow` with my own metal paint functions, possibly borrowing the clockwork kit's blotchy noise-based metal look for brass and iron surfaces.

I'm second-guessing whether importing `glow` from the kit path is safe, given uncertainty about how the harness resolves `agentic-3js-builder/kits/<name>` versus a single flattened import name—if only the top-level module is mapped, that subpath import could fail.

To stay safe, I'll just inline my own glow helper rather than depend on the kit import, caching modified emissive materials per mesh so cloning doesn't blow up memory for parts sharing the same base material.

Another concern surfaces: when the SDK's root getter bakes painted parts into a shared texture atlas, it may rebuild the material and texture map entirely for textured parts at read time, potentially overwriting whatever clone I set up.

The glow kit documentation confirms textured parts and cards glow with their texture's own colors, working through the atlas since the harness bakes everything into one mesh with one atlas carrying the emissive map — so the kit's approach should hold for both flat colors and textures. Since glow only applies to a handful of elements like gems or decals, I'm satisfied that's workable, and decal parts return as meshes so glow should apply fine there too.

Now I want to shift toward the actual creative direction — imagining a treasure-chest mimic with a long tongue, D&D style, starting with a big sturdy old chest as the base form.

I'm picturing the full design: worn planked wood with dark iron bands, rivets, and brass brackets; a lid propped open to reveal a fleshy pink-red interior with ridged palate, glaring yellow slit-pupil eyes, jagged teeth lining the rims, and drool strands hanging from the upper teeth with small beads at the ends; and a dark cavity at the rear suggesting a throat, possibly with a subtle glow.

I'm adding a treasure lure—coins and gems piled in the lower jaw and a few scattered near the tongue on the floor, kept modest—plus a thick rose-pink tongue with a central groove and bumpy papillae, curving out of the throat, over the lower front teeth, and drooping forward with a spiraled, hook-like tip.

Working out the tongue's path with Catmull-Rom control points, snaking forward in an S-curve from the throat over the lower lip to the floor, checking clearance against the jaw walls so it doesn't clip through the front teeth.

Continuing the path, the tip curls up near the end before rising further for a final flourish. Now I'm defining the tongue's cross-section as a flat ribbon shape, varying its width along the length.

The default path transport keeps the up-vector oriented so the tube's rx axis stays horizontal across the creature's right side initially, which confirms the frame behaves as expected along the path.

Now I'm thinking through the rigging: the tongue needs a chain built along the path, parented to a joint in the base skeleton, then swept with a radius function to form the actual geometry. I'm sketching out the skeleton hierarchy starting from a root body joint.

For naming, I want to use conventions a rigger would recognize—something like "hips" or "spine1" for the root, and "jaw" for the hinge joint that actually moves, since in this mimic creature the lid itself functions as the upper jaw while the base acts as the fixed lower jaw.

I'm reconsidering whether to label this joint `jaw` alone or add a separate `head` joint, since rig naming conventions expect recognizable chain roles like spine, neck, head, or jaw. Maybe it's cleaner to define an explicit `head` joint for this chest structure rather than overloading `jaw` with that role.

I'm also weighing whether to insert a `head` joint as a parent of `jaw` in the chain, since the root (hips) connects forward while the hinge sits at the rear of the base.

I'll treat the lid joint itself with a "jaw" role rather than "hinge," and I'm considering whether small eyelid joints would be worth adding for blinking, though that might be overengineering it.

Since materials are single-sided, viewing from below would cull the interior faces, so the hollow dome interior stays invisible while the eyeball underneath remains covered — that should be fine visually.

For angrier eyelids, I'm thinking about rotating the hemisphere around the eye's forward axis so the open edge tilts, lowering the inner corner. I'm working through the geometry: the sphere has radius 0.075, sitting just below the lid's palate surface in local coordinates, with the eyeball center positioned slightly beneath that palate plane before the pose transform is applied.

Checking the math, I'm computing the rotated direction vector after a 60-degree tilt, confirming the eye's forward axis ends up pointing nearly straight ahead so a viewer at the front sees the eyes looking directly at them. Now I'm turning to the interior structure of the lid for positioning the eyes.

Wait, recomputing the coordinates actually reverses my assumption — the lid's front rim with upper teeth ends up at the top after opening, not the bottom as I'd thought.

With the hinge at the back, the lid's front edge swings up and back, so at 60° open the front lip (closed-state front) sits behind the hinge's rim, and the viewer looking from the front sees the lid's underside, like a chest yawning open with its upper jaw tilted back — the gap is simply the chest's open mouth.

Mapping the view top to bottom: upper rim and teeth hang at the top pointing down, the palate with eyes sits below that angling toward the hinge, then there's a gap into the base's interior holding throat, tongue, and coins, with the lower teeth at the very front-bottom. I'm placing the eyes on the palate roughly mid-depth, around 40% of the way from the hinge toward the rim.

Checking the tongue's path from the throat upward and forward over the lower lip, confirming it stays well below the eyes so nothing overlaps. I'm also debating whether to add smaller secondary eyes alongside the two main ones for a more striking "mimic" look.

Now I'm thinking about the lid's other surfaces—since the model may be viewed from any angle, I should account for the exterior arch with its iron bands when seen from behind, and the lid's front edge face where the brass hasp and lip detail would be visible.

For the base interior, I want the mouth cavity to feel deep and cavernous, with the floor set back from the rim. I'm planning gum-pink ridge lining around the inside rim where teeth root, built from several strip-shaped parts along the front, left, and right edges.

I'm also designing the throat as a dark tunnel-like opening in the back wall, gradient from pink to black, possibly a hollow cone or cylinder, plus a small drooping uvula capsule hanging near the hinge on the palate for added gross detail.

I'm scattering a treasure pile across the mouth's floor — around 25 randomly oriented coin cylinders mounded together with assorted gems (octahedra, icosahedra in red, green, blue, gold) partially burying the tongue's base, playing into the classic mimic-with-loot trope to enrich the silhouette.

Capping the piece count to keep things manageable: roughly 30 coins, 8 gems, plus a few stuck to the legs and tongue. I'm positioning the pile toward the back half of the floor so it stays visible from a front-above viewing angle without completely obscuring the interior flesh around the rim and front teeth.

Now for the teeth: I'm designing an uneven mimic-style bite with a 7-tooth front row on the upper lid rim (heights varying 0.07–0.17) and smaller 4-tooth side rows, mirrored on the lower jaw but with a center gap for the tongue. I'll build each tooth as a cone-shaped sweep with reduced sides (5–6) for a jagged, fang-like look.

Writing tooth geometry helper...

So s[1] gives 0 at base and 1 at tip, meaning I can paint each tooth with a gradient from a yellowish-brown root to a bone-white tip using the uv coordinate. Though each tiny tooth part would occupy its own small chart in the paint sheet, so many tiny painted parts could strain the paint sheet's texel allocation.

Given the small surface area, chart padding overhead is a minor concern, so I'm leaning toward flat ivory/bone/yellowed/brownish color variants assigned randomly across teeth for a "dental neglect" look, since flat colors don't count against the 64-color budget the way paints might, though I need to double check how that budget is tracked.

Now I'm building out the full flat-color palette — ivory, bone, yellowed, dark iron tones, brass, flesh pinks and deep throat colors — assigning hex values to each named swatch.

I'm rounding out the gold and gem tones, then planning the paint groups (wood planks, flesh with veins, tongue, legs, iron, brass) and sketching the list of SVG textures needed: a detailed eye with iris, slit pupil, and highlights, likely reused across multiple eye instances with slight tint variations.

I'm now thinking about a decal for the lock plate — maybe an engraved brass emblem with a keyhole and filigree, possibly a playful d20 motif as a nod to tabletop gaming.

For the chest's wood texture, I'm weighing whether to use an SVG plank pattern with grain lines, knots, and nail heads mapped onto a box geometry, versus a simpler procedural paint-based stripe approach for the grain, since stretching across differently-sized faces could look uneven.

Actually, a position-based paint with plank seams, grain noise, and knot cells avoids stretching issues since it's defined in meters rather than UV space, keeping texture count down toward the 5-12 target. I'm starting to list out the texture set I'll need, beginning with the big yellow slit eye and a smaller contrasting eye color.

For the remaining textures, I'm considering a lock plate with filigree and keyhole, a runed iron band, and a clever trick where drool strands are rendered as cards hanging from tooth tips with solid pale-green shapes rather than translucent materials — cheap and effective using maybe eight along the upper rim and fewer on the lower.

I'm also weighing moss tufts and cobwebs in the corners to sell the dungeon-mimic vibe, though worried it might clutter the design, so I'm starting to draft a priority list starting with the bloodshot iris/pupil texture as the top item.

Continuing down that list: a brass lock plate with rivets and keyhole, arcane runes along the iron band (maybe as a plaque with a d20 on the lid front), plank textures for the chest body, drip cards for drool, and coin textures with a crown emblem mapped onto the cylindrical coin caps.

For coins specifically, I'm thinking of a grey-scale engraved texture (D20 or skull design) that gets tinted gold, silver, and copper to create material variety without needing three separate textures -- though each tint still eats its own atlas space.

I'm also sketching smaller detail textures: wart/pustule patterns for skin, sucker discs for pseudopods, a cobweb card for the lid corner, and maybe a tiny skull or bone pile as a fun dungeon-flavor detail among the victims' remains -- like a crushed helmet or skeletal hand caught in the mouth.

For the overall composition I'm settling on: the chest body with planks, bands, rivets and hardware; the maw with gums, teeth, palate, eyes and throat; the long bumpy tongue with a stuck coin; drool strands; four stubby clawed legs; two sucker-tipped pseudopod arms; and a treasure pile of coins, gems, and bones, with moss and grime painted into the wood grain for texture.

Now I'm roughing out the part count: walls, floor, and interior linings for the base, plus gum strips and trim boards get me to roughly eighteen pieces, then I'm working out the iron bands and corner brackets as separate strap and cap pieces to keep the geometry simple while still reading as riveted ironwork.

Moving to the lid, I'm counting shell, palate slab, end caps, bands, hasp, trim, and hinge barrels to land around fourteen parts, plus five curved ridge slabs for the palate. For the mouth I'm tallying eyes with lids and brows, upper and lower teeth with gum fillers, throat pieces, and the tongue with its papillae detail and embedded coin.

For drool, I'm realizing cards sharing one texture count as a single part regardless of quantity, so strands and beads collapse into just one or two part slots. Legs come out to roughly 36 parts across sweeps, foot pads, toes, and claws for all four, arms add about 28 with hands, fingers, and suckers, and the treasure pile of coins, gems, and bones tallies to around 41 parts.

I'm adding stuck coins and gems on the body, cobweb cards, iron ring handles, and moss cards, bringing the total to roughly 230-260 parts. For joints, I'm designing legs with hip, knee, and foot joints plus three toe joints each (24 total), arms with similar joint counts (14 total), plus hips, jaw, eyelids, and tongue joints, landing around 55 joints total—comfortably under the 160 limit.

Setting up imports...

I'm checking which exports come from each module—builder from one file, frame/line from another, math utilities like aim, lerp, mid, offset, rng, DEG, and vec from the math module, path helpers like arc, bezier, catmull, polyline, and spiral from the path module, limb from the ik module, and paint utilities like countershade, paint, spots, and stripes from the paint module, plus svg from texture. I'm also working out how rng(seed) should be typed and used as a parameter.

Now I'm estimating the painted surface area of the model to figure out the right texture resolution—summing up walls, lid, legs, tongue, and coins to get roughly 8 square meters of paintable surface, which suggests a texel density of about 3mm per texel at a given paint size, or finer if I bump up the resolution to 2048 or beyond.

I'm weighing whether to use a larger paint sheet size since narrow seam details (a few millimeters wide) risk being under-resolved at the default density, so widening the seams or increasing resolution would help, though I need to watch out for performance since baking millions of texels with noise functions in the browser could get slow.

I'll go with the default resolution and check that plank seam lines remain visible enough at that texel density, since they're only a couple texels wide. For detail level, I'll keep the default of 1 with 8-sided circle sweeps for a chunky low-poly look, then start sketching the character skeleton with the hip joint.

I'm setting the root joint at the base center with a "spine" role, keeping orientation simple since I'll mostly work in absolute model-space coordinates rather than local joint space. Since this model needs exactly one root joint, I place it with no parent, then add a jaw joint parented to the hips, positioned at the back top of the base with its bone pointing forward to form the lid's hinge.

For the jaw rotation, I'm working out the sign convention: rotating about the model's left axis (+X) by a negative angle tips the forward-pointing bone upward rather than down, which matches opening a jaw-like lid. Positive degrees would tip it down, so I need -62° to raise it correctly.

Now I'm setting up a tongue-like chain of nine joints parented to the hips, starting at the throat, using the default naming convention and checking how the chain's position-along-path parameter works.

For the count semantic, each knot span gets one joint by default, with resampling by arc length — so for a path through k points, I'd set count to roughly 10 to cover the spans evenly.

For the legs, I'm designing a function to build each leg per side and front/back, positioning the hip root slightly inside the base volume near each corner so the leg visually emerges from underneath. I'm planning each leg as a tapered thigh tube with a bulging knuckle, connecting to a shin and then a splayed three-toed claw foot, solved via inverse kinematics from hip to foot point.

Working through the IK math now: with hip and foot positions set and leg segment lengths of roughly 0.26 and 0.24, I calculate the reach distance and solve for how far the knee bulges perpendicular to the hip-foot line, bending outward and upward based on the hint direction.

The problem is that placing the knee outward and up pushes it right into the base's side wall at roughly its outer surface, which would look wrong — I'd rather have the knee splay outward and downward below the base, more like frog legs, so I need to reconsider the hint direction.

Actually, I think simpler stubby legs suit this creature better — four short, thick legs almost vertical beneath the base with a slight outward splay, like sturdy table legs ending in big clawed feet, rather than spindly spider-like limbs poking outside the footprint.

Setting base bottom at y=0.24 with height 0.40, rim at 0.64, total open-lid height around 1.45. For the silhouette, I like giving the legs a carved lion-paw chest foot look, but with a furry, bumpy mimic twist — thick legs tapering from radius 0.07 down to 0.055.

Coloring the limbs putty/grey-lilac with mottling, darker warty bumps, and lighter undersides, since mimics' true form is grey-brown fleshy pseudopods. I'm placing pseudopod arms rooted at the base's front side walls near (±0.55, 0.45, 0.12), curving outward and forward while rising, ending in hand-like pads with three finger-tentacles tipped in cream/pink suckers.

For the arms I'm giving each a four-joint chain (shoulder, elbow, wrist, tip), tapering radius from 0.06 to 0.04 over a length of about 0.7, with three two-jointed fingers per hand and small sucker discs scattered along the arm's underside. For the tongue I'm planning to scatter about 40 tiny papillae bumps across the top surface in a lighter pink to sell the slimy texture.

Thinking through part budget, I realize scattering 24 papillae instead of 40 is plenty since everything merges into a single mesh on export and I'm nowhere near the 1000-part cap even with the extra pieces. Now I'm sketching a wood-paint function that lays out planks with seams spaced along the vertical axis for horizontal-normal walls.

For the curved lid, plank seams need to follow the arch's angular direction rather than linear coordinates, so I'm working out how to derive the arc angle from surface position using the known hinge/center geometry, then use that angle to space seams evenly along the barrel curve.

For wood grain, I want streaks elongated along the plank direction, so I'm constructing a scaled position vector that compresses one axis before feeding it into the noise function — stretching features along x for horizontal planks on the z-facing walls.

I'm sketching a wood paint factory that takes light/dark/seam colors, plank size, seed, and optional arc parameters, then determines grain direction and plank boundaries based on which face normal dominates, similar to how I handled paneling earlier.

I also want to add small detail touches like darkened seams with subtle highlights, tiny nail-head dots staggered along plank ends, and patches of moss using noise-based smoothstep blending on upward-facing surfaces near edges—since small details like these are what make simple shapes feel convincing.

I'm also planning mud and dirt gradients near the base, directional warm/cool lighting tints depending on surface normal, and a general metal paint function for iron parts with rust speckles, scratches, and highlighted edges. Now I'm starting to define concrete geometry constants for the build.

Working out the lid's hinge position and local coordinate frame relative to the base's back wall, then sketching the arched outline of the lid using a superellipse-like curve in the z-y plane.

With p=2.6 the sides near the ends become near-vertical, which works well. I'm setting up the extrusion axes and hinge position so the shape extends forward in Z, computing the cross product to get the correct thickness direction.
